title: The commute
hook: travel time can be practice time

segments.voice: Yesterday, ending the workday: it was very good, and God ended; silence after Compline. Your line was done for today. Did the work get a clear edge? Today, the last day of the week. Day nine hundred twenty-four.

A train car in the morning, rows of heads bent over glowing screens. A line of cars at a red light. A bus window streaked with rain. Between the start of the workday and its end there's a stretch that belongs to neither home nor work, and it's easy to treat it as time to be killed. Henry David Thoreau, in his essay Walking, says he has met hardly anyone who understood the art of walking, who had, as he puts it, a genius for sauntering. Then he tells a story about where that word came from. Today: the commute.
screen: `HEADS BENT OVER SCREENS.` → `TIME TO BE KILLED?` → `A GENIUS FOR SAUNTERING.`

segments.voice: First, Thoreau's story. He says saunter comes from idlers in the Middle Ages who roamed the country asking for charity on the pretense of going to the Holy Land, à la Sainte Terre, until children cried, there goes a Sainte-Terrer, a saunterer, a Holy-Lander. Whether or not a dictionary agrees with him, his point is clear: a walk can be a small pilgrimage. Second, a psalm for the trip. In the King James Bible, Psalm 121 ends: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore." Going out and coming in: the whole commute fits in one line. Third, a prayer for the road. Jewish tradition has Tefilat HaDerech, the traveler's prayer, said when setting out on a journey, asking to be brought to the destination in peace and returned in peace. The road itself is treated as a place where something deserves to be said. Fourth, the steps. In the Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha teaches that when walking, a practitioner knows, I am walking. Some Buddhists practice walking as a meditation of its own, attention resting in the feet. Put together, travel time can be practice time. Not every trip allows it in the same way: a driver's practice is full attention on the road. But a walk, a train, a bus, a passenger seat can be a stretch of quiet between the two halves of a day. This week ran through work's corners: envy, a difficult boss, mistakes, a craft, a beginning and an ending. The commute is the road that connects them.
screen: `SAINTE-TERRER: A HOLY-LANDER.` · `THY GOING OUT AND COMING IN.` · `A PRAYER FOR THE ROAD.` · `WHEN WALKING, KNOW IT.` · then, large: `THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Picture the trip you make most often: the door, the street, the station or the car. Imagine making it once with the phone left in a pocket or a bag. What would you see? Let three things from the route come to mind: a tree, a corner, a face you pass. If you drive, picture the road itself, held in full attention. If you pray, you can bring the going out and the coming in to God in your own tradition's words. Then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
The commute. The going out and the coming in, which can be practice time instead of time to be killed. Today's word.
Your line: the road. On your next trip to work, or anywhere, leave the phone in your pocket for the whole way once, and see what the road shows you. Day nine hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Jews say Tefilat HaDerech, the traveler's prayer, when setting out on a journey; some Buddhists practice walking meditation; Christians and Jews read Psalm 121 as a psalm for travelers.

fork.setup: you're on foot, heading somewhere ordinary, with the phone in your pocket. Thoreau has one word for doing this well. which?
fork.reveal: sauntering, which he traces, playfully, to Sainte-Terrers: travelers bound for the Holy Land.

original.note: Hebrew: the prayer of the road, the traveler's prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: the commute is dead time between home and work.
what it means: travel time that can become practice time: attention, a breath, a small pilgrimage.
what a scholar hears: Thoreau's Walking, which plays on saunter as Sainte-Terrer, a Holy-Lander, beside Psalm 121:8 on the going out and the coming in.

notes: Thoreau's Walking paraphrased: 'met with but one or two persons... who had a genius, so to speak, for sauntering' (softened to 'hardly anyone') and his derivation of saunter from Sainte-Terrer. The lesson flags that a dictionary may not agree; confirm that framing is fair.

Tefilat HaDerech: described as said when setting out on a journey, asking to arrive and return in peace; source given as Berakhot 29b–30a from memory. A Judaism Keeper should confirm the source, and whether to note that it is customarily said for journeys beyond a city's limits rather than a daily commute.
Satipatthana Sutta paraphrased ('when walking, he knows I am walking'); a Buddhist Keeper should confirm.
Week-end day (924): the teach's close looks back on days 918–923.
